So, I work in IT for a fairly large corporation, and while I'm not involved with directly supporting end users in anyway, I have "IT" in my title, so that means it's ok for folks to call, email, chat, or barge into my office instead of contacting the service desk. I'm sure many of you understand.

Anyway, received an email from one of the summer interns that she and the other intern were having trouble with an IP address they were assigning to some device. Since she was a student from my alma mater, I decided to take a look. When I tracked them down, they told me they couldn't ping the static IP the network admin had given them for their device, which was still neatly packed up in its box on the floor.

WARNING WARNING. I shrugged it off, since there was a laptop sitting on the floor, connected with a LAN cable right next to it, I just assumed that they configured the laptop for their static address and were not able to ping it.

Bad assumption. It turns out, they had been trying to ping the IP without configuring it for any device and since they were not getting a response, were going cube to cube with their laptops (set for DHCP) "searching" for the static IP, so they would know which network drop to plug their device into. I explained how the individual network drops were not assigned IPs and that the IP should be configured in their device, which could be plugged in anywhere. Since they both looked very skeptical, I set her laptop to use the static address and had the other intern ping it to show their was no network issue.

I felt like I had saved the day, but she became visibly upset and told me she didn't want to have to move her desk here...apparently she believed that this was the only network drop her computer could connect through now and wouldn't believe otherwise until I set it back to DHCP and let her plug it back in at her desk.

TL;DR: An intern with a 4.0 GPA and three years of a computer science program under her belt doesn't understand basic networking.
